description: A timeline comparison of major crypto exchanges’ fiat-valued asset volumes during the 2022–2025 shockwave: top platforms consolidated while fragile players failed, triggering cascading withdrawals, insolvencies, and market-share resets.
youtube_description:
🎬 Crypto’s “exchange collapse season” didn’t happen all at once—it happened in chapters.

In this chart-race style video, we track fiat-valued exchange asset volumes (USD billions) across five major platforms from 2019 to 2026—showing how withdrawals, insolvencies, and regulatory pressure reshaped the map.

⏱️ Chapters
00:00 The pre-shock growth (2019–2021): Binance and OKX surge
01:05 2022: The market cracks, confidence fractures
02:20 The FTX implosion moment (late 2022): a giant hits $0
03:15 2023–2024: Survivors consolidate and rebuild user trust
04:40 2025–2026: The new “safe-but-fast” era forms

📌 What you’ll see
• Binance climbs through the turbulence to become the dominant consolidated survivor
• Coinbase and Kraken steady-share while compliance becomes a competitive advantage
• OKX grows as liquidity migrates away from the collapsed platforms
• FTX rockets into the chart… then falls off a cliff after its collapse

👍 If you enjoyed this visualization, like, subscribe, and comment “RACE” for the next timeline comparison.

instagram_caption:
🚨 The crypto exchange “collapse season” didn’t just wipe out a company… it reshuffled the entire leaderboard.

Picture this: from 2019 to 2021, the exchange world looked invincible. Binance went from about $8.5B (2019) to $44.0B (2021). OKX followed with a jump from $1.6B to $9.6B in the same window—while Coinbase climbed from $3.1B to $15.5B. Even “smaller survivors” like Kraken were growing fast (from $1.2B to $4.8B). The theme was simple: more users, more volume, more momentum.

Then 2022 hit like a storm front. Binance still rose—from $44.0B (2021) to $52.6B (2022). Coinbase pushed higher too, hitting $22.8B. But the real drama was the shadow hanging over the system: FTX was still huge heading into 2022, at roughly $22.0B in this timeline—big enough to be a central node in the market.

And then—boom. The FTX collapse moment shows up brutally in the chart: FTX goes from $22.0B (2022) to $0.0B in 2023, staying there through 2024, 2025, and 2026. One platform disappears, and the “liquidity vacuum” becomes a transfer machine. After that cliff, Coinbase rises to $27.2B (2023) and $31.4B (2024), while Kraken climbs steadily to $11.4B (2024) and $13.8B (2026). Binance continues compounding, reaching $74.5B by 2026, and OKX grows into the post-shock era (from $13.9B in 2022 to $26.8B by 2026).

So here’s the real question: in a crisis, do you think “trust + liquidity” wins (Binance/Coinbase style), or do you think the next wave of challengers will come from places that look smaller today?

Comment your pick—and follow for more timeline chart-races that make market history feel like a movie.
facebook_caption:
The crypto market’s exchange landscape was transformed by the 2022–2023 shockwave. This visualization compares fiat-valued exchange asset volumes (USD billions) for Binance, Coinbase, OKX, Kraken, and FTX from 2019 to 2026.

Key turning point: FTX. It reached approximately $22.0B in 2022, then collapsed to $0.0B by 2023 and remained at zero through 2026—an abrupt destruction of a major liquidity hub. Meanwhile, the “survivor” exchanges consolidated.

Binance increased from about $44.0B (2021) to $74.5B (2026). Coinbase rose from $15.5B (2021) to $37.6B (2026). OKX climbed from $9.6B (2021) to $26.8B (2026), and Kraken grew from $4.8B (2021) to $13.8B (2026). The overall story is a dramatic transfer of volume toward platforms that retained liquidity and credibility as the industry de-risked.
